title: Karl Benz and the Patent-Motorwagen
summary: Karl Benz grew up poor, the son of a train driver who died when he was a baby. After years of money troubles, he built a light, three-wheeled machine with a little petrol engine at the back, and in 1886 he got a patent for it. When he first drove it through the streets of Mannheim, people stared, laughed or ran away, but it was the start of the automobile age.

sections.heading: A Train Driver's Son in Karlsruhe
paragraphs: On 25 November 1844, in Mühlburg, a village that is now part of the city of Karlsruhe in south-west Germany, a baby boy was born to a young woman named Josephine Vaillant. He was named Karl Friedrich Michael Vaillant. A few months later his mother married the boy's father, Johann Georg Benz, and the child took his father's name. The world would come to know him as Karl Benz (his name is also often spelled Carl).

Johann Georg Benz was a locomotive driver on the railways of the Grand Duchy of Baden. It is easy to imagine little Karl hearing stories of hissing engines, coal smoke and the thrill of speeding along the tracks. But he never got to know his father well. When Karl was only two years old, Johann Georg died; family accounts say he caught pneumonia after working out in the cold and wet. Josephine was left alone to raise her son with very little money.

She was determined that Karl would have the best education she could manage, even though the family lived close to poverty. Money was tight, and she made sacrifices so that he could stay in school instead of going out to work. Karl repaid her by doing very well. At the Lyceum, a demanding secondary school in Karlsruhe, he was a top student, especially good at science and mathematics. He loved locks, clocks and machines, and he is said to have earned pocket money by repairing watches and making photographs, both very modern hobbies for the 1850s.

At the age of just 15, Karl passed the entrance exam for the Polytechnic school in Karlsruhe, one of the best engineering colleges in Germany, and began studying mechanical engineering. He graduated in 1864, aged 19. Years later, when he wrote his life story, Benz said that even as a student he had dreamed about a vehicle that could move without horses and without rails. At the time, the only machines that could pull loads by themselves were steam locomotives like the ones his father had driven, and those needed tracks.

sections.heading: Wandering Years and an Iron Workshop
paragraphs: Graduating was one thing. Finding a good job was another. For about seven years after college Benz moved from firm to firm, gaining practical experience but never quite settling. He worked as a fitter and draughtsman for engineering firms in Karlsruhe, Mannheim and Pforzheim, and briefly in Vienna. He learned how iron was cast, cut, shaped and bolted together, and how a drawing on paper became a real machine. These were exactly the skills he would need later.

In 1871, aged 26, he decided to work for himself. Together with a partner named August Ritter, he started an iron foundry and mechanical workshop in Mannheim, a busy trading city on the river Rhine. It went badly almost from the start. Ritter turned out to be unreliable, orders were scarce, and before long the authorities seized the company's tools because it could not pay its debts. For a young engineer with big dreams, it was a disaster.

Help came from Pforzheim. Benz had met Bertha Ringer, the daughter of a wealthy master builder and carpenter in that town. Bertha was clever, practical and very interested in technology. Before they were married, she used part of her dowry, the money a bride's family provided when she married, to buy out Ritter's share of the business. That move saved the workshop and put Karl back in control.

Karl and Bertha were married on 20 July 1872. Under German law at the time, once a woman married she could no longer act on her own as a business investor; her money and legal rights were counted as her husband's. Bertha's support, though, never stopped. She kept the household going through years of worry, ran the home, raised their five children, Eugen, Richard, Clara, Thilde and Ellen, and stood behind Karl's experiments when others thought he was wasting his time. Part 5 tells the story of her most famous day; in this part, remember that without her money and determination, there might have been no car at all.

The 1870s were hard years in Germany. A financial crash in 1873 hit businesses all over the country, and Benz's little workshop struggled to find customers for its sheet-metal and machine work. He needed a product that would actually sell. He decided it should be an engine.

sections.heading: New Year's Eve, 1879
paragraphs: Otto's four-stroke engine was protected by a patent, as you saw in Part 3, so Benz could not simply copy it. Instead he worked on a different design called a two-stroke engine, which makes a power stroke every time the crankshaft goes round once, instead of every second time. He hoped that selling stationary engines to workshops would finally bring in a steady income and pay for his bigger dream.

The work dragged on for months. According to the story Benz later told, on New Year's Eve 1879, after supper, he and Bertha went to the workshop to try the engine one more time. This time it started, and it kept running, with a steady beat that Benz later compared to music. Whether or not every detail of the tale is exact, the date is well recorded: the engine was finished at the end of 1879 and patented in 1880.

Building the engine forced Benz to solve many practical problems, and he patented a number of the parts he developed for it and for his later engines, including his own designs for the spark plug, the carburettor that mixes fuel with air, the clutch and the radiator. Each of these would be needed in a car.

Even so, money was still a problem. The banks that lent to Benz insisted that his business become a company with shareholders. In 1882 it was reorganised as the Gasmotoren-Fabrik Mannheim, the Mannheim Gas Engine Factory. But Benz was left owning only about five percent of the shares, and the other owners were not interested in his ideas for vehicles. Frustrated, he left after only about a year.

In 1883 he tried again. With two new partners, Max Rose and Friedrich Wilhelm Esslinger, who ran a bicycle repair business, he founded a new firm called Benz and Cie., the Rheinische Gasmotorenfabrik in Mannheim. At first it made stationary gas engines, which sold well enough that the company grew quickly. For the first time in years, Karl Benz had a steady business, a workshop, skilled workers and a little time. He used it to build the vehicle he had dreamed about since his student days.

sections.heading: Not a Carriage With an Engine, but a Whole New Machine
paragraphs: Many inventors before Benz had taken an ordinary horse carriage, bolted an engine onto it and hoped for the best. Benz did something different. He started with a blank sheet of paper and designed the engine, the frame, the wheels, the steering and the drive as parts of one single machine, each made to suit the others. That is one big reason historians treat his vehicle as the first true automobile powered by an internal combustion engine.

Look at the Patent-Motorwagen, which means patent motor carriage, from the side and it looks almost like a giant tricycle with a bench seat. Its frame was made of light steel tubes, the same kind of construction used for bicycles, which were becoming popular in the 1880s. It ran on three large wheels with thin wire spokes: two at the back and one at the front. Why only three? Steering two front wheels at once was a tricky problem in those days, because on a curve the inner and outer wheels need to turn by different amounts. Benz was not happy with the steering methods used on carriages, so for his first cars he avoided the problem by using a single front wheel. (Part 9 explains how engineers later solved two-wheel steering properly.) He steered it with a small crank handle on a vertical post, connected to the front wheel by a little toothed rack and gear.

Behind the bench seat, low down between the rear wheels, sat the engine. It was a single-cylinder, four-stroke engine running on the same principle as Otto's, but it was far smaller and lighter than the big iron factory engines of Deutz. Its cylinder held about 954 cubic centimetres, a little less than a one-litre carton of milk, and later measurements show it turning at about 400 revolutions per minute, about twice as fast as a typical stationary Otto engine of the time. It produced roughly three-quarters of a horsepower, about 0.55 kilowatts. That is less power than a modern ride-on lawn mower, and less than the horse it was meant to replace.

Lying flat above the engine was a big horizontal flywheel, a heavy spinning wheel that stored energy between the engine's power strokes and kept it turning smoothly. Laying it flat, rather than upright like on a factory engine, kept the machine low and compact, and it is often said that Benz chose this layout so that the spinning wheel would not disturb the steering.

The fuel was ligroin, a light, easily evaporating petroleum liquid similar to the white spirit or naphtha sold as a cleaning solvent. It was fed into a simple surface carburettor, a container in which air passed over the fuel and picked up vapour, making a burnable mixture. To light that mixture, Benz did not use Otto's little gas flame. He used electric ignition: a battery and a trembler coil produced a high-voltage spark inside the cylinder. Electric ignition was more reliable and better suited to a moving vehicle, and Benz had worked hard on it.

An engine that burns fuel inside gets very hot, so it must be cooled. Benz surrounded the cylinder with a water jacket. As the engine worked, the water heated up, boiled and simply escaped as steam, so the car had to stop now and then for its water to be topped up. This is called evaporative cooling. It was simple, but it meant that water, as much as fuel, limited how far the car could go.

Finally, the power had to reach the wheels. From the engine, a leather belt drove a cross-shaft under the seat. Moving the belt from a loose pulley to a fixed one worked like a simple clutch, letting the driver start and stop the wheels without stopping the engine. The cross-shaft contained a differential, so that the two rear wheels could turn at different speeds on a bend, and from each end of it a chain, like a bicycle chain, drove one of the rear wheels. There was only one speed and no reverse gear. To stop, the driver pulled a hand lever that pressed a brake against the drive. The whole machine was much lighter than any steam carriage and could be started in a few minutes. Starting the engine meant heaving on the flywheel by hand.

sections.heading: How Do You Drive a Machine Nobody Has Driven Before?
paragraphs: Today, starting a car usually means pressing a button. In 1886 it was a small adventure, and there were no driving instructors, because nobody except Benz and his workers had ever done it. Let us imagine climbing aboard a Motorwagen and going through the steps, based on how the machine was built.

First come the checks. Is there enough water in the cooling jacket? If not, the engine will soon overheat. Is there ligroin in the fuel container that feeds the carburettor? The car carried only a few litres, so it could not go very far between fill-ups, and in 1886 there were no filling stations anywhere in the world. Is the battery for the ignition connected and charged? Without its spark, the engine is just a lump of metal.

Next, the engine has to be started, and there is no electric starter motor to help. The driver stands beside the car and turns the big horizontal flywheel by hand, giving it a strong swing so that the piston is pulled through its intake and compression strokes. If the fuel mixture is right and the spark arrives at the right moment, the engine catches with a bang and then settles into a steady chuffing rhythm. If not, the driver tries again, and again.

Now the driver climbs onto the bench seat. The engine is running, but the car is still standing still, because the drive belt is on its loose pulley, spinning freely. Pushing a lever slides the belt across onto the fixed pulley, and the car begins to creep forward as the belt grips. Steering is done with the small crank on top of the vertical column, turning the single front wheel left or right. There is no steering wheel yet, no speedometer, no lights, no windscreen and no roof. On a cold or rainy day, driver and passenger simply got cold and wet.

Stopping takes planning too. Pulling the lever back slips the belt onto the loose pulley again, disconnecting the engine from the wheels, and a hand brake slows the car. The brakes were weak, the wheels were thin and hard, and every bump in the cobbled streets came straight up into the seat, because the earliest version had very little in the way of springs. Going downhill was nerve-racking. Going uphill was often worse, because with less than one horsepower and a single gear the car could slow to a crawl or stop altogether on a steep slope.

Compare that with a horse. A strong horse can work harder than this whole engine for a short time, it can find its own way home, and it does not need a mechanic. But a horse must be fed, watered, groomed and stabled every single day, even on days when it does no work at all, and it gets tired. The Motorwagen used fuel only while it was running and, in theory, could keep going as long as its fuel and water lasted. That was the promise that made Benz keep going: a tireless horse made of steel. All it needed now was more power, better gears, stronger brakes and someone brave enough to take it far from home.

sections.heading: The Birth Certificate of the Automobile
paragraphs: On 29 January 1886 Karl Benz applied to the Imperial Patent Office in Berlin for a patent on his invention. He described it as a vehicle with gas engine operation, in German Fahrzeug mit Gasmotorenbetrieb. (In those days, the word gas engine was often used for any engine that burned a vapour or gas, including petrol vapour.) The patent was granted on 2 November 1886 and given the number DRP 37435. DRP stands for Deutsches Reichspatent, German Imperial Patent.

The patent document is short: a few pages of text and a sheet of careful technical drawings showing the three-wheeled vehicle from the side and from above. It does not claim to have invented the engine, or the wheel, or the carriage. Its claim is for a whole vehicle driven by its own small engine, with the engine and vehicle designed to work together. Because of that, many people call DRP 37435 the birth certificate of the automobile.

The document has become so famous that in 2011 it was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register, a list of documents considered especially important to the history of all humanity. It sits there alongside treasures such as the Gutenberg Bible and Beethoven's Ninth Symphony.
A patent, though, does not make anyone buy a car. Benz still had to show that his strange machine actually worked, and he had to convince people that they wanted one.

sections.heading: Laughs and Shrieks on the Ringstrasse
paragraphs: Benz's first test drives took place in and around his workshop yard in Mannheim during 1885 and early 1886. They were short, nervous trips. The engine stalled, parts broke and had to be redesigned, and one early test reportedly ended with the machine running into a wall. Each time, Benz went back to the workshop, made improvements and tried again.

On 3 July 1886 he drove the Motorwagen in public on the Ringstrasse, the ring road around the centre of Mannheim. Imagine the scene. A summer street full of horse-drawn wagons, people walking, children playing, dogs and the occasional cyclist on a high-wheeled bicycle. Suddenly, with a rattling, popping, puffing sound and a smell of burning fuel, a carriage comes along with no horse in front of it at all, steered by a serious man in a hat gripping a little crank handle.

People's reactions were not what an inventor would hope for. Some stared in astonishment. Some laughed at the odd, spindly contraption and made fun of it. Horses shied, and some passers-by were frightened, thinking that a carriage moving by itself must be dangerous or even unnatural. The local newspapers mentioned it, but few people seemed to understand that they had just seen the beginning of something enormous. Many simply assumed it was a curiosity that would soon be forgotten, like so many other inventions they had read about.

Benz also faced practical limits. Local rules did not yet have any category for a motor vehicle, so he needed permission from the authorities for his drives, and the car's range was limited by how much fuel and water it could carry. Its top speed was about 16 kilometres per hour, roughly 10 miles per hour. That is faster than walking, about the speed of a jogging adult or a gently pedalled bicycle, but slower than a horse at full gallop.

He kept improving the design. Improved versions followed, the Model II and the Model III, with sturdier bodies, larger engines and more power, and later a second speed. Sales began in 1888, and one of the very first buyers was Émile Roger, a Paris bicycle maker who also sold Benz engines and cars in France. In 1889 a Benz Model III was shown at the great World's Fair in Paris, the same exhibition for which the Eiffel Tower was built, but it found very few buyers. Only a handful of Patent-Motorwagens were made in the first few years.

Today the vehicle has a quieter life. A Patent-Motorwagen rebuilt in the 1890s from Benz's first car has been on display in the Deutsches Museum in Munich since 1906. An early production car can be seen in the Science Museum in London, and many replicas have been built so that people can see, hear and even ride in this little machine that started so much.

sections.heading: Fair Credit: Many Hands on the Wheel
paragraphs: So did Karl Benz invent the car? It is better to say this: Karl Benz built and patented the first practical automobile powered by an internal combustion engine, designed from the beginning as one complete vehicle. That is a huge achievement. But he was not working alone in an empty world.

Think back over the story so far. Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot's steam fardier had moved under its own power in 1770, and British steam coaches had carried passengers on real roads decades before Benz was born. François Isaac de Rivaz had fitted a hydrogen engine to a crude cart around 1808. Étienne Lenoir had driven his Hippomobile to Joinville-le-Pont in about 1863. Benz's engine worked on the four-stroke principle first described by Alphonse Beau de Rochas and first built as a practical engine by Nicolaus Otto. In Vienna, Siegfried Marcus was experimenting with petrol-powered carts, though the dates of his surviving car are still debated.

Most strikingly, only about 100 kilometres away in Cannstatt, Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach were working in their garden workshop at the very same time. In 1885 and 1886 they built their own small, fast engine, mounted it on a wooden two-wheeler and then on a four-wheeled carriage. As far as we know, the two teams worked separately, and Daimler and Benz probably never met. You will meet their machines in Part 6. Inventions often happen like this: when the right parts and ideas become available, several people in different places race toward the same goal at once.

What made Benz's work special was the way it combined everything: a light, fast-running petrol engine, electric ignition, a carburettor, water cooling, a differential and chain drive, all built into a frame designed for them. He also had the patience to keep improving it, and a growing company to build and sell it. Later, Benz and Cie. would become one of the largest carmakers in the world, and in 1926 it merged with Daimler's company to form Daimler-Benz. Karl Benz lived until 1929, long enough to see motor cars filling the streets that had once laughed at him.

But in 1888 all of that was still in the future. Sales were tiny. Newspapers were unimpressed. Karl, who was a careful, sometimes anxious man, was not at all sure the world would ever want his car, and he is said to have hesitated to take it out on long trips in case something went wrong in front of everyone. Someone needed to show the public that this machine was not just a toy for driving around a workshop yard, but something that could carry real people on a real journey. And at home in Mannheim, his wife Bertha was quietly making a plan to prove exactly that.

deepDive: Why do historians argue about the first car, and why does Benz usually win? It depends on the definition. If a car is any self-propelled road vehicle, Cugnot's steam fardier of 1769 to 1770 came first. If it must have an internal combustion engine, de Rivaz's hydrogen cart around 1808 and Lenoir's Hippomobile around 1863 have claims, and supporters of Siegfried Marcus once argued for an even earlier date, though most historians now date his surviving car to about 1888 or 1889. Benz's claim rests on a combination of features: a light, purpose-built vehicle; a compact four-stroke engine running on liquid petroleum fuel, which could be carried on board rather than piped from a gas main; electric ignition; a patent clearly describing the whole concept; and, crucially, the start of production and sales. That last point matters. Many earlier machines were one-off experiments; Benz's design founded a continuous line of development that leads directly to modern cars. The numbers show how modest the start was. The engine's swept volume was about 954 cubic centimetres, yet it produced only around 0.75 horsepower at about 400 rpm. Modern tests on reconstructions have given figures between roughly 0.7 and 0.9 horsepower, so the exact output depends on the engine's condition and fuel. A modern small car engine of similar size might produce 50 to 70 kilowatts, about a hundred times more, thanks to higher compression, faster running speeds, better fuel mixing and precise electronic ignition. Benz's top speed of about 16 km/h was limited not just by power but by the single gear: the belt and chain ratios had to be low enough for the engine to move the car at all, so the car could not go faster without the engine racing beyond its safe speed. This is exactly the problem that multi-speed gearboxes later solved, and one Bertha would discover first-hand on the hills on the road to Pforzheim. Finally, it is worth noticing whose name is not on the patent. Bertha Benz helped fund the work, but married women in Germany at the time had very limited legal rights over property and business, so the patent is in Karl's name alone. Historians today increasingly describe the Motorwagen as a family achievement.
funFact: Karl Benz's 1886 patent, DRP 37435, is listed in UNESCO's Memory of the World Register, which means the paperwork for his three-wheeled car is officially treated as a treasure of world heritage.
